Ephesians
eh-FEE-zhunz
noun (proper)
From Greek Ephesioi (Ἐφέσιοι) — the inhabitants of Ephesus, the great Aegean port city and provincial capital of Roman Asia; title of Paul's most architecturally structured epistle, spanning eternal election through domestic order and spiritual warfare.

Biblical Definition

The Epistle to the Ephesians is one of Paul's four prison letters, composed from Rome circa AD 60–62. Its structure is precisely bipartite: chapters 1–3 are doctrinal (the eternal purpose of God in the church through Christ) and chapters 4–6 are practical (the life befitting that election). The doctrinal half opens with a sustained doxology of electing grace: God chose His people “in Him before the foundation of the world — that we would be holy and blameless before Him” (Eph 1:4), predestined them to adoption, redeemed them by His blood, and sealed them with the Spirit. Salvation is framed with the defining formula: “For by grace you have been saved through faith — and that not of yourselves; it is the gift of God” (Eph 2:8). The mystery revealed through the gospel is the creation of one new body from Jew and Gentile, united in Christ — the church as God's display of manifold wisdom before the principalities and powers (Eph 3:10). The practical half commands wives to be subject to their own husbands “as to the Lord” (Eph 5:22) — a submission modeled on the church's submission to Christ and therefore theologically constitutive, not culturally contingent. It closes with the call to put on the full armor of God against rulers, powers, and spiritual forces of wickedness (Eph 6:11–12). The 1689 LBCF draws on Ephesians for its doctrines of election, the church, and complementarian household order.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster does not record “Ephesians” as a common English noun; it names the recipients of Paul's canonical circular letter and the most systematically complete Pauline doctrinal epistle, spanning from eternal election to household order.

expand to see more

EPHESIANS, n. pl. [From Ephesus, the chief city of the Roman province of Asia.] The inhabitants of Ephesus; specifically, the recipients of Paul's prison epistle — likely a circular letter to the churches of Asia Minor, spanning the full arc from eternal election to domestic order.

Reformed theology reads Ephesians as the doctrinal center of Paul's prison correspondence: its monergistic soteriology, high ecclesiology, household code, and spiritual-warfare cosmology together provide the scaffolding for confessional church life in every age.

Calvin's commentary on Ephesians and the Westminster Confession's doctrine of election both draw directly from Ephesians 1 — chosen before the foundation of the world, predestined according to the good pleasure of God's will, sealed with the Spirit as the earnest of inheritance.

Key Scripture

Eph 1:4 — "According as he hath chosen us in him before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and without blame before him in love:"

Eph 2:8 — "For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God:"

Eph 5:22 — "Wives, submit yourselves unto your own husbands, as unto the Lord."

Eph 6:12 — "For we wrestle not against flesh and blood, but against principalities, against powers, against the rulers of the darkness of this world, against spiritual wickedness in high places."

Modern Corruption

Egalitarian revisionism targets the Ephesians household code as a culturally conditioned appendage; progressive readings dissolve its complementarian structure into mutual submission without ordered headship.

expand to see more

The principal modern corruption of Ephesians concentrates on its household code (5:22–6:9). Egalitarian interpreters (CBE International, the “Christians for Biblical Equality” movement, Gordon Fee) argue that Eph 5:21 (“submitting to one another”) governs the household code mutually, rendering wifely submission indistinguishable from husbandly submission. This dissolves the text's own analogy (wife-to-church, husband-to-Christ), both of which are ordered rather than mutual in structure. A church that submits to Christ as Christ also submits to the church is not the relationship Ephesians describes.

The monergistic soteriology of Ephesians 2 faces a parallel assault: Arminian and open-theist readings reinterpret election as conditional on foreseen faith, and “dead in trespasses and sins” (Eph 2:1) as a figure of speech rather than a description of the will's bondage. Reformed orthodoxy holds that Ephesians 2 describes total depravity and monergistic regeneration: God makes the dead alive; the faith He requires He also supplies (Eph 2:8). Any reading that makes the sinner a co-initiator of salvation departs from the letter's grammar and its explicit “not of yourselves” (2:8).

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Rooted in the name of the ancient Ionian city Ephesus and the Greek charis (“grace”) — the controlling theological term that binds together election, redemption, and spiritual gift throughout Paul's most structured letter.

expand to see more

Ephesus — the chief city of Roman Asia, site of the temple of Artemis and Paul's three-year ministry (Acts 19); likely the editorial center from which this circular letter reached the Lycus Valley churches

Greek charis (χάρις) — grace, unmerited favor; the animating principle of Ephesians — sinners saved by grace (2:8), gifts given by grace (4:7), warfare sustained by His mighty power (6:10)

Greek mysterion (μυστήριον) — mystery, secret now revealed; the Jew-Gentile union in one body is the mystery hidden in ages past but now disclosed through the gospel proclamation (3:3–6)

Greek panoplia (πανοπλία) — full armor; the military metaphor of Eph 6:11–17, describing the believer's complete God-supplied equipment for cosmic spiritual combat

Greek proorisas (προορίσας) — having predestined; from Eph 1:5, the term the Reformed tradition cites to establish unconditional election as Pauline doctrine, not Augustinian invention

Usage

"Ephesians 1:4–11 is the Reformed church's primary locus for the eternal decree of election — chosen in Christ before the foundation of the world, predestined according to the good pleasure of God's will, not according to foreseen merit or anticipated faith."

"The household code of Ephesians 5:22–6:9 is the complementarian church's principal New Testament text: headship and submission are theological categories grounded in the Christ-and-church relation, not cultural accidents to be revised with changing social expectations."

"The spiritual-warfare passage (Eph 6:10–18) grounds the believer's conflict in cosmic reality — the enemy is not flesh and blood but spiritual powers — and supplies the armor entirely from God's provision, establishing that Christian perseverance is supernatural, not therapeutic."
